title: Rate Limiting Algorithms
objectives: Protect services by capping requests per key using token bucket, leaky bucket or sliding windows.
Answer: HTTP status for rate limited?

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: Token bucket: tokens refill at rate r up to capacity b; each request spends one — allows bursts. Sliding window counters smooth boundary spikes. Store counters in Redis for a shared limit.

cards.body: Protect services by capping requests per key using token bucket, leaky bucket or sliding windows.

title: Distributed Unique IDs
objectives: Generate unique IDs at scale: UUIDs, DB sequences, Snowflake, or ticket servers.
Answer: Why not public auto-increment IDs?

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: UUIDv4 is random and needs no coordination but indexes poorly. Snowflake 64-bit IDs (timestamp + worker + sequence) are sortable. UUIDv7 adds time ordering.

cards.title: The core idea
cards.body: Generate unique IDs at scale: UUIDs, DB sequences, Snowflake, or ticket servers.

cards.title: How a request flows
cards.body: 5 steps from “Timestamp bits” to “Sortable 64-bit ID”, via “Worker ID bits”.

cards.title: Watch out for
cards.body: Using auto-increment IDs exposed publicly — leaks volume and enables enumeration.

questions.prompt: Which ID is 64-bit and sortable by time?
questions.explanation: Timestamp bits come first.

questions.prompt: Snowflake has a 12-bit sequence per millisecond per worker. Roughly how many IDs per second can one worker make?
Why do random UUIDv4 primary keys hurt B-tree inserts?

choices.label: Inserts land at random places in the index, splitting pages and hurting caching

questions.explanation: Time-ordered IDs (UUIDv7, Snowflake) insert at the end.

questions.prompt: Public order URLs look like /orders/1043, from an auto-increment id. Main risk?

choices.label: Anyone can guess other ids and estimate your order volume

questions.explanation: Sequential ids leak volume and invite enumeration.

questions.prompt: IDs for orders created on 50 app servers.

rationaleOptions.label: Worker bits avoid coordination
The timestamp prefix sorts by creation time
UUIDv4 is time-sortable

rationaleConflicts.r3: v4 is random; UUIDv7 is the time-ordered variant.

questions.explanation: Snowflake gives both properties.

flashcards.back: Time-ordered UUID.
Leak volume, enable enumeration.

title: 2PC & Saga
objectives: Explain two-phase commit and why it blocks

cards.title: Two-phase commit
cards.body: A coordinator asks every participant to prepare (lock and promise), then tells all to commit or all to abort. It gives atomicity across databases, but participants hold locks while waiting, and if the coordinator dies after prepare they are stuck.

cards.title: Sagas
cards.body: A saga splits the work into local transactions, one per service. If a later step fails, earlier steps are undone by compensating actions (refund, release the seat). No global locks, but the system is briefly inconsistent.

cards.title: A trip booking saga
cards.body: 5 steps from “Reserve flight” to “Compensate: cancel flight”, via “Reserve hotel”.

cards.title: Choreography vs orchestration
cards.body: Choreography: each service reacts to the others’ events; no central brain, but the flow is hard to see. Orchestration: a coordinator calls each step and runs compensations; easier to follow and change.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Defaulting to 2PC across microservices. It ties every service’s availability together and holds locks across network calls. Prefer sagas unless you truly need atomic commit.

questions.prompt: Main drawback of two-phase commit?

choices.label: Participants hold locks and can be stuck if the coordinator fails after prepare

questions.explanation: Blocking is the price of atomic commit.

questions.prompt: Order two-phase commit.
questions.explanation: Locks are held from prepare to commit.

questions.prompt: A saga’s payment step fails after the flight and hotel were reserved. What happens?

choices.label: Compensating actions cancel the hotel and then the flight
The database rolls back all three automatically
The saga retries the payment forever

questions.explanation: Sagas undo with new actions, in reverse order.

questions.prompt: Which is orchestration?

choices.label: A booking coordinator calls flight, hotel and payment in turn and runs compensations
The client calls each service itself
Each service listens for the previous service’s event and reacts

questions.explanation: A central coordinator owns the flow.

questions.prompt: Checkout spans order, payment and inventory services.

rationaleOptions.label: Sagas keep data consistent at every instant
Compensations undo partial work
Services stay available independently

rationaleConflicts.r3: Sagas are briefly inconsistent between steps; design for it.

questions.explanation: Sagas trade instant consistency for availability.

flashcards.back: Participants hold locks and can be stuck if the coordinator fails after prepare. Blocking is the price of atomic commit.

flashcards.front: A saga’s payment step fails after the flight and hotel were reserved. What happens?
flashcards.back: Compensating actions cancel the hotel and then the flight. Sagas undo with new actions, in reverse order.
A booking coordinator calls flight, hotel and payment in turn and runs compensations. A central coordinator owns the flow.

title: Outbox Pattern & CDC
objectives: Use change data capture to publish database changes

cards.title: The dual-write problem
cards.body: A service saves an order and then publishes OrderPlaced to Kafka. If it crashes between the two, the order exists but nobody hears about it; if the publish succeeds and the database write fails, consumers act on an order that does not exist.

cards.title: Transactional outbox
cards.body: Write the order and an outbox row in the same database transaction. A relay reads unsent outbox rows, publishes them to the broker and marks them sent. Either both are saved or neither is.

cards.title: Outbox to broker
cards.body: 5 steps from “BEGIN” to “Relay publishes to Kafka and marks them sent”, via “Insert the order and an outbox event”.
steps: Insert the order and an outbox event
Relay publishes to Kafka and marks them sent

cards.title: Change data capture
cards.body: CDC tools such as Debezium tail the database’s write-ahead log and turn each committed change into an event. No polling and no app changes; it can publish the outbox table or any other table.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Forgetting the relay delivers at least once. It can crash after publishing but before marking the row sent, so consumers must handle duplicates idempotently.

questions.prompt: A service writes an order to its database, then publishes to Kafka, and crashes in between. Result?

choices.label: The order exists but no event was published

questions.explanation: Two separate writes are not atomic.

questions.prompt: How does the outbox pattern avoid the dual-write problem?

choices.label: It publishes to Kafka before writing to the database
The event is saved in the same transaction as the data, then relayed
It uses two-phase commit between the database and Kafka
It retries the publish from memory until it works

questions.explanation: One local transaction, then an at-least-once relay.

questions.prompt: Order the outbox flow.

items.label: Insert the order and an outbox event
Relay publishes and marks them sent

questions.explanation: The relay runs after commit.

questions.prompt: How does CDC capture changes?

choices.label: By intercepting HTTP requests to the service
By asking each developer to publish events
By reading the database’s write-ahead log
By running SELECT * on every table each second

questions.explanation: The log already has every committed change.

questions.prompt: The relay publishes an event, then crashes before marking it sent. What happens next?

choices.label: The database rolls back the order
It publishes the event again, so consumers must be idempotent

questions.explanation: At-least-once relays create duplicates.

flashcards.front: A service writes an order to its database, then publishes to Kafka, and crashes in between. Result?
flashcards.back: The order exists but no event was published. Two separate writes are not atomic.

flashcards.front: How does the outbox pattern avoid the dual-write problem?
flashcards.back: The event is saved in the same transaction as the data, then relayed. One local transaction, then an at-least-once relay.
By reading the database’s write-ahead log. The log already has every committed change.

flashcards.front: The relay publishes an event, then crashes before marking it sent. What happens next?
flashcards.back: It publishes the event again, so consumers must be idempotent. At-least-once relays create duplicates.

title: Consensus & Raft
objectives: Walk through a Raft write and election
Size a cluster for a number of failures

cards.title: What consensus solves
cards.body: Several nodes must agree on one ordered log of commands even when some crash. Raft and Paxos do this; etcd, Consul and ZooKeeper use them to hold config, locks and leader information.

cards.title: Raft in brief
cards.body: One leader accepts writes, appends them to its log and replicates them to followers. An entry is committed once a majority has stored it. If followers stop hearing heartbeats, one starts an election for a new term and wins with a majority of votes.

cards.title: A Raft write
cards.body: 5 steps from “Client sends the write to the leader” to “Leader commits and applies it”, via “Leader appends it to its log”.
steps: Client sends the write to the leader
Leader appends it to its log

cards.title: Majorities and fault tolerance
cards.body: N nodes need a majority, floor(N/2) + 1, so they tolerate floor((N − 1)/2) failures: 3 nodes survive 1, 5 survive 2. Even sizes add cost without adding tolerance.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Running consensus on 2 nodes, or putting a high-latency link in every write. Two nodes cannot lose one and keep a majority, and every commit waits for the slowest member of the majority.

questions.prompt: How many failures does a 5-node Raft cluster tolerate?
questions.explanation: A majority of 3 must stay up.

questions.prompt: Smallest cluster that tolerates 3 failures with majority quorums?
Order a Raft write.

items.label: Client sends the write to the leader
Leader appends it to its log

questions.explanation: Commit needs a majority, not everyone.

questions.prompt: Followers stop receiving heartbeats from the leader. What happens?

choices.label: The cluster waits until the old leader returns
A follower starts an election for a new term and needs a majority of votes
The lowest-id follower takes over without a vote

questions.explanation: Terms and majority votes prevent two leaders.

questions.prompt: Why run 3 nodes rather than 4?

choices.label: Four nodes split every vote evenly forever
Four nodes cannot elect a leader
Four nodes still tolerate only one failure but need three acknowledgements per write

questions.explanation: Majority of 4 is 3, so tolerance stays at 1.

flashcards.front: How many failures does a 5-node Raft cluster tolerate?
flashcards.back: 2. A majority of 3 must stay up.

flashcards.front: Followers stop receiving heartbeats from the leader. What happens?
flashcards.back: A follower starts an election for a new term and needs a majority of votes. Terms and majority votes prevent two leaders.
Four nodes still tolerate only one failure but need three acknowledgements per write. Majority of 4 is 3, so tolerance stays at 1.

title: Leader Election & Distributed Locks
objectives: Coordinate exclusive access across services with leases, fencing, and caution.

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: Redis SET NX PX gives a simple lock with TTL; ZooKeeper/etcd give safer locks. Always bound locks with TTLs and design for lock loss.

cards.title: The core idea
cards.body: Coordinate exclusive access across services with leases, fencing, and caution.

cards.title: How a request flows
cards.body: 5 steps from “Request lock” to “TTL auto-expires on crash”, via “SET key NX PX”.

cards.title: Watch out for
cards.body: Holding a lock without a TTL — a crashed holder blocks everyone forever.

cards.title: Fencing tokens
cards.body: A lock holder can pause (GC, network) past its lease while another node takes the lock. Give each grant an increasing token and make storage reject writes with an older token, so a paused former holder cannot corrupt data.

cards.title: Leader election
cards.body: Leader election is a long-lived lock: one node wins a lease in etcd or ZooKeeper, renews it while healthy, and another takes over when it expires. Use it for singletons such as a scheduler.

questions.prompt: Why must a distributed lock have a TTL?

choices.label: To spread load across Redis nodes
To make acquiring the lock faster
To let the same holder lock twice
So a crashed holder does not block everyone forever

questions.explanation: Leases expire on their own.

questions.prompt: Lease TTL is 10 s; the holder hits a 12 s GC pause. Without fencing, how many nodes may believe they hold the lock at once?
questions.formula: The pause outlasts the lease, so a second node acquires the lock while the first still thinks it owns it: 2.
questions.workedAnswer: The pause outlasts the lease, so a second node acquires the lock while the first still thinks it owns it: 2.
questions.explanation: The pause outlasts the lease, so a second node acquires the lock while the first still thinks it owns it: 2.

questions.prompt: How does a fencing token stop a paused former lock holder?

choices.label: Redis replicates the lock to every node
The lock service kills the old holder’s process
Storage rejects writes carrying a token older than the newest it has seen
The token makes the lease never expire

questions.explanation: Safety is enforced where the data lives.

questions.prompt: Order safe lock usage.

items.label: Acquire the lock with a TTL
Do the work, sending the token with each write
Release the lock (or let it expire)

questions.explanation: The token travels with the writes.

questions.prompt: Run a nightly billing job once across 50 workers.
constraints: Exactly one worker should run it

approaches.label: Leader election through an etcd lease, with fencing
Redis SET NX without a TTL

rationaleOptions.label: A lock without a TTL is safest because it never expires
Fencing stops a paused former leader from writing
Only the lease holder runs the job

rationaleConflicts.r3: A crashed holder would then block the job forever.

questions.explanation: Leases plus fencing handle both crashes and pauses.

flashcards.back: SET key value NX PX ttl.
Update only if current value matches expected.

title: Lamport & Vector Clocks
objectives: Wall clocks drift; use logical clocks (Lamport, vector) or hybrid clocks for ordering.

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: NTP-synced clocks can skew by milliseconds. Lamport clocks give a causal total order; vector clocks detect concurrency. Snowflake-style IDs combine time + machine + sequence.

cards.title: The core idea
cards.body: Wall clocks drift; use logical clocks (Lamport, vector) or hybrid clocks for ordering.

cards.title: How a request flows
cards.body: 5 steps from “Event on A” to “Causal order preserved”, via “Increment counter”.

cards.title: Watch out for
cards.body: Using server timestamps to decide "last write wins" across regions without accounting for skew.

questions.prompt: Which can tell that two updates were concurrent?
questions.explanation: Lamport clocks give an order but cannot detect concurrency.

questions.prompt: Node B has counter 7 and receives a message stamped 12. B’s new counter?
Two regions use server time for last-write-wins and region B’s clock runs 50 ms fast. Risk?

choices.label: B’s older writes can beat A’s newer ones

questions.explanation: Skew decides the winner, not real order.

questions.prompt: Order a Lamport clock exchange.

items.label: A sends a message with its counter
B sets its counter to max(own, received) + 1

questions.explanation: Receivers jump ahead of what they have seen.

questions.prompt: What does a Lamport clock guarantee?

choices.label: If A’s timestamp is smaller, A happened before B
If A happened before B, A’s timestamp is smaller

questions.explanation: The implication only goes one way.

flashcards.back: Timestamp + machine ID + sequence.
Wrong ordering for last-write-wins.

title: Gossip & Failure Detection
objectives: Explain how gossip spreads cluster state
Compare fixed timeouts with phi-accrual detection

cards.title: Gossip
cards.body: Every second each node picks a few random peers and swaps what it knows: membership, heartbeats, versions. News reaches the whole cluster in about log N rounds with no central server, which is why Cassandra and Consul use it.

cards.title: Failure detection
cards.body: Nodes send heartbeats. A fixed timeout declares a node dead after one missed beat and flaps during GC pauses. Phi-accrual detectors output a suspicion level from recent arrival times, so slow-but-alive nodes are not evicted.

cards.title: One gossip round
cards.body: 5 steps from “Node picks random peers” to “Cluster converges”, via “They exchange state with version numbers”.
steps: They exchange state with version numbers

cards.title: Suspect before dead
cards.body: SWIM-style detectors ask other nodes to ping a silent node before marking it suspect, then dead. Indirect checks avoid blaming a node for one bad network path.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Declaring a node dead on one missed heartbeat. A GC pause triggers a rebalance, the node comes back, and data moves twice.

questions.prompt: Gossip reaches N nodes in roughly how many rounds?
questions.explanation: Each round roughly doubles who knows.

questions.prompt: Each node tells one random peer per round, so the number who know roughly doubles. About how many rounds to reach 1,000 nodes?
questions.explanation: 2^10 = 1,024, so about 10 rounds.

questions.prompt: What does a phi-accrual detector output?

choices.label: A suspicion level based on recent heartbeat timing
Dead or alive after one missed heartbeat

questions.explanation: A level lets you pick a threshold per use.

questions.prompt: Node A cannot reach node C. Before marking C dead, a SWIM-style detector:

choices.label: Waits for C’s next leader election
Asks other nodes to ping C indirectly

questions.explanation: One bad path should not condemn a node.

questions.prompt: Order one gossip round.
questions.explanation: Versions decide what is newer.

flashcards.front: Gossip reaches N nodes in roughly how many rounds?
flashcards.back: O(log N). Each round roughly doubles who knows.

flashcards.front: What does a phi-accrual detector output?
flashcards.back: A suspicion level based on recent heartbeat timing. A level lets you pick a threshold per use.

flashcards.front: Node A cannot reach node C. Before marking C dead, a SWIM-style detector:
flashcards.back: Asks other nodes to ping C indirectly. One bad path should not condemn a node.

title: Bloom Filters/HyperLogLog/Count-Min
objectives: Choose the right probabilistic structure for a question
State the error each one makes

cards.title: Answers that are almost right
cards.body: At billions of items exact answers get expensive. Probabilistic structures trade a small, known error for tiny memory: kilobytes instead of gigabytes.

cards.title: Which one when
cards.body: Bloom filter: “have I seen this?” (false positives possible, no false negatives). HyperLogLog: “how many distinct?” (about 1% error in ~12 KB). Count-Min Sketch: “how often?” (may overcount, never undercounts).

steps: Definitely new: fetch and add to filter

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Using a Bloom filter where a false positive is harmful, such as deciding a username is taken. A false positive there blocks a real user; confirm against the database.

choices.label: A hash set of every visitor id

questions.explanation: HLL estimates distinct counts in kilobytes.

choices.label: It is probably not in the set
It is definitely not in the set
It might be there; check the database

questions.explanation: Bloom filters have false positives, never false negatives.

questions.prompt: Track how often each search term appears per minute in tiny memory. Which?

choices.label: A sorted set of every term

questions.explanation: Count-Min answers “how often”, possibly overcounting.

title: Timeouts/Retries/Circuit Breakers
objectives: Set timeouts that fit the caller’s deadline
Use circuit breakers and bulkheads to contain failures

cards.title: Timeouts
cards.body: Every outbound call needs a timeout shorter than the caller’s own deadline. Without one, threads wait forever on a hung dependency and the caller runs out of threads too.

cards.title: Retries
cards.body: Retry only idempotent operations, a few times, with exponential backoff and jitter. Retries at every layer multiply: 3 attempts at each of 3 layers is up to 27 calls.

cards.title: Circuit breakers
cards.body: Closed: calls flow and failures are counted. Open: after too many failures, calls fail fast without trying. Half-open: after a cooldown, a few trial calls decide whether to close again.

cards.title: A breaker through an outage
cards.body: 5 steps from “Closed: calls flow” to “Trials succeed: closed again”, via “Failures pass the threshold”.

cards.title: Bulkheads
cards.body: Give each dependency its own pool of threads or connections, so a slow recommendations service cannot use up the pool checkout needs.

questions.prompt: After the cooldown, a circuit breaker enters:

choices.label: Closed: all calls flow at once

questions.explanation: Trials decide whether to close.

questions.prompt: Three layers each make up to 3 attempts. Worst case, how many calls reach the bottom service for one user request?
questions.formula: Each attempt above triggers up to 3 below: 3^3
questions.workedAnswer: Each attempt above triggers up to 3 below: 3^3 = 27 calls.
questions.explanation: Each attempt above triggers up to 3 below: 3^3 = 27 calls.

questions.prompt: A dependency hangs and no timeout is set. What happens to the caller?

choices.label: The operating system retries the call
Its threads pile up waiting until it cannot serve anyone

questions.explanation: Hung calls spread the outage upward.

questions.prompt: Order a breaker through an outage and recovery.
questions.explanation: Fail fast while it is down.

questions.prompt: Checkout calls a flaky recommendations service.

approaches.label: Retry many times with no timeout
Timeout, circuit breaker and a default fallback, in its own pool

rationaleOptions.label: Failing fast while it is down keeps threads free
Checkout must not wait on an optional feature
More retries help the dependency recover faster

rationaleConflicts.r3: Extra retries add load to a struggling service and slow its recovery.

questions.explanation: Contain optional dependencies so they cannot take checkout down.

flashcards.front: After the cooldown, a circuit breaker enters:
flashcards.back: Half-open: a few trial calls. Trials decide whether to close.

flashcards.front: A dependency hangs and no timeout is set. What happens to the caller?
flashcards.back: Its threads pile up waiting until it cannot serve anyone. Hung calls spread the outage upward.

title: Logs/Metrics/Traces
objectives: Metrics show what, logs show details, traces show where across services.

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: Track RED (rate, errors, duration) for services and USE (utilisation, saturation, errors) for resources. Correlate with a trace ID propagated through every hop.

cards.title: The core idea
cards.body: Metrics show what, logs show details, traces show where across services.

cards.title: How a request flows
cards.body: 5 steps from “Request gets trace ID” to “Dashboards & alerts”, via “Each service logs it”.

cards.title: Watch out for
cards.body: Logging everything at DEBUG in production with no structure or sampling.

questions.prompt: Best tool to find which of 8 services slowed down one request?

choices.label: Grepping each service’s logs by timestamp

questions.explanation: Spans show time spent per hop.

questions.prompt: RED metrics for a service are:
questions.explanation: Service-level health in three numbers.

questions.prompt: Which is a USE metric for a database disk?

choices.label: Saturation, such as the I/O queue depth
Requests per second to the API

questions.explanation: USE (utilisation, saturation, errors) is for resources.

questions.prompt: Order how observability data flows.
questions.explanation: The trace id ties it together.

questions.prompt: Production logs everything at DEBUG as free text. Problem?

choices.label: Huge volume and cost, and hard to query

questions.explanation: Structure and sample logs.

flashcards.back: Logs, metrics, traces.
99% of requests are faster than this.

title: Availability & SLAs
objectives: Availability is uptime percentage; each extra nine cuts allowed downtime by 10×.

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: 99.9% ≈ 8.8 h/year down, 99.99% ≈ 53 min/year. Components in series multiply availability (lower); redundant components in parallel raise it. SLO = internal target; SLA = contractual promise.

cards.title: The core idea
cards.body: Availability is uptime percentage; each extra nine cuts allowed downtime by 10×.

cards.title: How a request flows
cards.body: 5 steps from “Single node” to “Health checks + failover”, via “Find SPOFs”.

cards.title: Watch out for
cards.body: Claiming five nines without redundancy across zones. Availability comes from removing single points of failure.

questions.prompt: Two services in series, each 99.9% available. End-to-end availability?
questions.explanation: 0.999 × 0.999 ≈ 0.998, assuming independent failures.

questions.prompt: Allowed downtime per year at 99.9% availability, in hours?
Two independent replicas, each 99% available, with instant failover. Availability?
questions.explanation: Both must fail: 0.01 × 0.01 = 0.0001, so availability is 1 − 0.0001 = 0.9999.

questions.prompt: SLO versus SLA?

choices.label: SLA is measured per request, SLO per year
SLO is the internal target; SLA is the promise to customers, with penalties
SLA is the internal target; SLO is the customer promise

questions.explanation: Set the SLO tighter than the SLA.

questions.prompt: Order the path to higher availability.
questions.explanation: Remove single points of failure step by step.

flashcards.back: ≈ 52.6 minutes.
Series multiplies (lower); parallel redundancy raises it.

title: Disaster Recovery & Multi-Region
objectives: Define RPO and RTO and derive them from business needs
Explain the data cost of cross-region replication

cards.title: RPO and RTO
cards.body: RPO: how much data you can lose, measured in time (the last 5 minutes of writes). RTO: how long until service is back. Both are business decisions that set the design and the cost.

cards.title: Strategies
cards.body: Backup and restore: cheapest, hours of RTO. Pilot light: data replicated, minimal servers ready to scale. Warm standby: a smaller full copy running. Active-active: every region serves traffic; lowest RTO, hardest consistency.

cards.title: Regional failover
cards.body: 5 steps from “Mumbai region fails health checks” to “Fail back after the incident”, via “DNS or a global load balancer shifts traffic”.
steps: DNS or a global load balancer shifts traffic

cards.title: Data across regions
cards.body: Async replication between regions keeps writes fast but means RPO above zero: the last seconds of writes can be lost. Synchronous cross-region writes give RPO zero at tens of ms per write.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Never testing failover. Backups that were never restored and runbooks that were never run tend to fail on the day. Rehearse with game days.

questions.prompt: The business can lose at most 5 minutes of orders. Which number is this?
questions.explanation: RPO is data loss; RTO is downtime.

questions.prompt: Cheapest DR strategy when hours of RTO are acceptable?
questions.explanation: Nothing runs until you need it.

questions.prompt: Order a regional failover.
questions.explanation: Promote data before scaling.

questions.prompt: Cross-region replication is asynchronous. Consequence on failover?

choices.label: The last seconds of writes may be lost (RPO above zero)
Every write gets slower by one round trip

questions.explanation: Async trades a small data-loss window for fast writes.

questions.prompt: DR for a payments app: RTO under 5 minutes, RPO near zero.
constraints: Writes can afford a few extra ms

approaches.label: Warm standby with synchronous replication to the nearby region
Async replication to a far region only

rationaleOptions.label: Synchronous replication keeps RPO at zero
Nightly backups meet a 5-minute RTO
A running standby can take traffic within minutes

rationaleConflicts.r3: Restoring from backups takes hours and loses up to a day of data.

questions.explanation: Targets drive the strategy.

flashcards.front: The business can lose at most 5 minutes of orders. Which number is this?
flashcards.back: An RPO of 5 minutes. RPO is data loss; RTO is downtime.

flashcards.front: Cheapest DR strategy when hours of RTO are acceptable?
flashcards.back: Backup and restore. Nothing runs until you need it.

flashcards.front: Cross-region replication is asynchronous. Consequence on failover?
flashcards.back: The last seconds of writes may be lost (RPO above zero). Async trades a small data-loss window for fast writes.

title: AuthN vs AuthZ
objectives: Prove who the user is: server sessions, signed tokens, or delegated OAuth/OIDC.

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: Sessions store state server-side (easy revoke). JWTs are signed, stateless, short-lived with refresh tokens. OAuth 2.0 delegates access; OIDC adds identity.

cards.title: The core idea
cards.body: Prove who the user is: server sessions, signed tokens, or delegated OAuth/OIDC.

cards.title: How a request flows
cards.body: 5 steps from “Login with OTP” to “Refresh when expired”, via “Verify”.

cards.title: Watch out for
cards.body: Long-lived JWTs with no revocation path.

cards.title: Authentication vs authorization
cards.body: Authentication answers who you are (password, OTP, passkey, Sign in with Google). Authorization answers what you may do: can this user refund this order? Authenticate once per session; authorize on every request, close to the data.

questions.prompt: A logged-in support agent tries to refund an order from another region and is blocked. Which check stopped them?
questions.explanation: They proved who they are; they lacked permission for this action.

questions.prompt: Biggest drawback of long-lived stateless JWTs?

choices.label: They cannot be verified without the auth server
They are hard to revoke before they expire
They are too small to carry claims

questions.explanation: Nothing server-side remembers them.

questions.prompt: Why might a bank prefer server-side sessions over JWTs?

choices.label: A session can be revoked instantly by deleting it on the server
Every service verifies sessions without a lookup

questions.explanation: Server state makes revocation easy.

questions.prompt: Order a token-based login.

items.label: Call APIs with the access token

questions.explanation: Short access tokens, longer refresh tokens.

questions.prompt: Where should “can this user refund this order?” be checked?

choices.label: In the service that owns orders, on every request

questions.explanation: UI checks are convenience; the service enforces.

flashcards.back: Long-lived token to get new short-lived access tokens.
Who you are vs what you can do.

title: OAuth 2.0 & OIDC
objectives: Walk through the authorization code flow with PKCE
Choose token types for web and mobile

cards.title: Two jobs, two specs
cards.body: OAuth 2.0 lets an app act on your behalf with limited scopes (“read my Google Drive files”). OpenID Connect adds an ID token on top so the app also learns who you are: “Sign in with Google”.

cards.title: Code flow with PKCE
cards.body: The app redirects to the identity provider, gets a short-lived code back, and exchanges it, plus a PKCE verifier, for tokens over a back channel. PKCE stops a stolen code being redeemed by another app.

cards.title: Sign in with Google
cards.body: 4 steps from “App redirects to Google with code_challenge” to “App exchanges code + verifier for ID and access tokens”, via “User logs in and consents”.
steps: App redirects to Google with code_challenge
Google redirects back with a code
App exchanges code + verifier for ID and access tokens

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Using an OAuth access token as proof of identity. It says what the app may do, not who the user is. Use the OIDC ID token for login.

questions.prompt: Why do mobile apps use PKCE?

choices.label: A stolen authorization code cannot be redeemed without the app’s secret verifier
It removes the need for HTTPS
It lets the app read the user’s password

questions.explanation: The verifier proves the redeemer started the flow.

questions.prompt: To log a user in with Google, which token proves who they are?
questions.explanation: Access tokens say what the app may do, not who the user is.

questions.prompt: An app asks to “read your Google Drive files”. What is this?

choices.label: OAuth 2.0 delegated access with a limited scope

questions.explanation: Scopes limit what the app can do on your behalf.

questions.prompt: Order “Sign in with Google” with PKCE.

items.label: App redirects to Google with a code challenge
Google redirects back with a code
App exchanges code + verifier for tokens

questions.explanation: Tokens come over the back channel.

questions.prompt: A fintech aggregator reads bank statements on a user’s behalf.
constraints: Users must be able to revoke access
The app should never see bank passwords

approaches.label: Ask users for their bank password

rationaleOptions.label: The user grants limited, revocable access
Storing passwords is fine if they are encrypted
The app never handles the bank password

rationaleConflicts.r3: With the password the app can do anything as the user, and access cannot be scoped or revoked separately.

questions.explanation: Delegation beats impersonation.

flashcards.back: OAuth grants delegated access; OIDC adds identity via an ID token.
An intercepted authorization code being redeemed by another app.

flashcards.front: Which token proves who logged in?
flashcards.back: The OIDC ID token.

title: JWT
objectives: Explain what a JWT contains and who can read it

cards.title: Signed, not secret
cards.body: A JWT is header.payload.signature, base64-encoded. Anyone holding it can read the claims; the signature only proves they were not changed. Never put secrets in the payload.

cards.title: Why services like it
cards.body: Any service with the public key can verify a token without calling the auth server, so verification scales horizontally and survives an auth outage.

cards.title: Verifying a request
cards.body: 4 steps from “Client sends Authorization: Bearer token” to “Passes user claims to service”, via “Gateway checks signature with public key”.
steps: Gateway checks signature with public key

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Week-long access tokens. A stateless token cannot be easily revoked, so keep access tokens short (minutes) and use refresh tokens, which can be revoked server-side.

questions.prompt: A teammate wants to put the user’s PAN in the JWT payload “because it is signed”. What is wrong?

choices.label: Anyone holding the token can decode it; signing only stops changes
Only the gateway can read the payload
The token becomes too large to sign

questions.explanation: Signed, not secret.

questions.prompt: A user logs out but their access token is valid for 7 more days. Which design limits this best?

choices.label: Short-lived access tokens with revocable refresh tokens

questions.explanation: Keep the window of a stolen token small.

questions.prompt: Why can 20 services verify JWTs without overloading the auth server?

choices.label: The auth server pushes sessions to all of them
Each verifies the signature with the public key, without a call
Tokens are verified only at login

questions.explanation: Verification is local.

questions.prompt: Order JWT verification at the gateway.

items.label: Gateway checks the signature with the public key
Gateway checks exp, aud and iss
Gateway passes user claims to the service

questions.explanation: Signature first, then claims.

questions.prompt: Besides the signature, what should verification check?
questions.explanation: A valid signature on an expired or foreign token is still a reject.

flashcards.front: Can anyone read a JWT payload?
flashcards.back: Yes. It is signed, not encrypted.

flashcards.front: Why are JWTs easy to scale?
flashcards.back: Services verify them locally with a public key, no auth-server call.

flashcards.front: How do you limit damage from a stolen JWT?
flashcards.back: Short expiry plus revocable refresh tokens.

title: Security Essentials
objectives: Layer defences so one failure is not a breach
Handle secrets and permissions with least privilege

cards.title: Defence in depth
cards.body: Assume any one layer fails. Combine TLS in transit, authentication, authorization on every request, input validation, rate limits, encryption at rest and audit logs.

cards.title: Injection
cards.body: Never build SQL or shell commands from user input. Use parameterised queries, and validate input. One string-concatenated query can leak a whole table.

cards.title: Secrets
cards.body: Keep API keys and passwords out of code and images. Load them from a secrets manager at runtime, scope each to one service, and rotate them.

cards.title: A request through the layers
cards.body: 5 steps from “TLS at the edge” to “Validate input and run a parameterised query”, via “Rate limit and web firewall”.
steps: Validate input and run a parameterised query

cards.title: Least privilege
cards.body: Give each service and person only the access they need: a read-only database user for reporting, a bucket policy for one prefix. A breach then exposes less.

questions.prompt: Search builds SQL as "… WHERE name = '" + input + "'". Fix?

choices.label: Wrap the same concatenation in a stored procedure
Strip quotes from the input with a regex

questions.explanation: Parameters keep data from being parsed as SQL.

questions.prompt: Where should a payment-gateway API key live?

choices.label: In a secrets manager, loaded at runtime and rotated

questions.explanation: Code and images get copied; secrets must not travel with them.

questions.prompt: The reporting service only reads orders. Its database user should have:

choices.label: Read-only access to the tables it needs
Write access in case it needs it later

questions.explanation: Limit what a compromise can do.

questions.prompt: Order the layers a request passes through.
questions.explanation: Each layer catches what the previous missed.

questions.prompt: HTTPS is enabled everywhere. Is the API secure?

choices.label: Not by itself: you still need authentication, authorization, validation and rate limits
Yes, once the CDN is enabled
Yes, as long as certificates are renewed

questions.explanation: TLS is one layer of several.
